tagline: Land of smiles, temples, and street food
overview:
Thailand sits at the center of mainland Southeast Asia, bordering Myanmar, Laos, Cambodia and Malaysia, with a long tail of land running down the Malay Peninsula between the Andaman Sea and the Gulf of Thailand. At about 513,000 km² it is roughly the size of Spain.

About 70 million people live in Thailand and nearly all speak Thai, a tonal language written in a looping alphabet with no spaces between words. Bangkok, the capital, is a vast, hot, energetic city of canals, temples, markets and elevated trains; its full ceremonial name is the longest place name in the world.

Thailand is a constitutional monarchy, and the king is deeply respected. The country is the only one in Southeast Asia never colonized by a European power, a fact Thais take pride in. Rice farming, factories and tourism support the economy, and Thai food has become one of the world's favorite cuisines.
landAndNature: Forested mountains rise in the north around Chiang Mai, where Doi Inthanon reaches 2,565 meters and winter nights are cool. The center is a flat, wet plain of rice paddies watered by the Chao Phraya River, one of the world's great rice-growing regions. The northeast, called Isan, is a drier plateau. In the south, limestone karst towers erupt from turquoise water at Phang Nga and Krabi, hiding caves and hidden lagoons, and coral reefs ring islands like Phuket and Koh Tao. The monsoon brings heavy rain from May to October. Wild elephants, gibbons, hornbills and the occasional tiger live in national parks, and the Mekong giant catfish, which can weigh 300 kilograms, swims the northern river.
peopleAndCulture: Thai greetings use the wai, palms pressed together with a small bow, and heads are considered the highest part of a person while feet are the lowest, so pointing feet at someone is rude. Most Thais are Buddhist, and many young men spend time as monks; temples with gilded roofs and spirit houses outside buildings are everywhere. Food balances sweet, sour, salty and spicy: pad thai noodles, green curry, som tam papaya salad pounded in a mortar, and mango with sticky rice. Muay Thai, boxing that uses fists, elbows, knees and shins, is the national sport, opened with a slow dance of respect. Songkran in April is a nationwide water fight marking the traditional new year, and Loy Krathong floats candlelit baskets on rivers.
history: People have farmed and made bronze in this region for thousands of years; Ban Chiang's pottery is more than 4,000 years old. Thai-speaking peoples moved south and founded the kingdom of Sukhothai in the 1200s, where the Thai alphabet was created. Ayutthaya, founded in 1351, grew into one of the largest and richest cities in the world, trading with China, Japan, Persia and Europe, until Burmese armies destroyed it in 1767. A new capital was built at Bangkok in 1782 under the Chakri dynasty, which still reigns. Kings Mongkut and Chulalongkorn modernized the country and used careful diplomacy to stay independent while Britain and France colonized their neighbors. Absolute monarchy ended in a 1932 revolution, and the name changed from Siam to Thailand in 1939. Politics since has included many military coups.
funFacts: Bangkok's full ceremonial name has 168 letters in Thai and is recognized as the longest place name in the world.
Thailand was never colonized by a European power, unlike every one of its neighbors.
During Songkran in April, whole cities turn into a three-day water fight with buckets, hoses and water guns.
The Thai alphabet has 44 consonants and no spaces between words, so readers work out where each word ends.
Thailand is one of the world's biggest exporters of rice, and Thai has a word meaning 'to eat rice' that simply means to eat.
